item.title: What Is a Parent’s Job, Really?
item.description:
Motivation

What Is a Parent’s Job, Really?

Rethinking our goals for raising happy and successful children.

Posted August 17, 2026

Key points
  • A clear parent job description helps parents lead with purpose rather than react to a child’s distress.
  • Parenting goals can focus on character and maturity rather than happiness and success.
  • Children need loving support—and enough space to develop responsibility and independence.
  • Mature parenting focuses on managing ourselves rather than trying to manage our children.

This article draws on excerpts from my recent book, The Parenting Paradox (Bloomsbury, 2026).

Book Cover
Source: Bloomsbury

Can you imagine starting a new job with an organization and discovering that you have no job description? You’re given a title—one of great importance—but no clear goals, no outlined responsibilities, no measurable tasks. No orientation or training, either. This is essentially what parents face when they commence their first day in their new and vital role—holding a tiny, helpless infant in their arms.

It’s striking to me that almost all parenting courses for expectant parents focus solely on baby care, rather than the broader role of guiding parents through their child’s growing years. Courses for expectant parents—often called antenatal classes or prenatal education—prioritize preparing parents for childbirth, early parenting, and the fundamentals involved in the physical care of a baby in the first few months.

I recall that my husband and I attended such a course at the hospital where our first child was to be born. We even had a plastic baby to practice diaper changing, swaddling, and other similar practical tasks. We hung on every word of the midwife and prepared ourselves diligently for the arrival of baby number one. So much focus on birth prep and so little on what the heck to do with the dramatic changes to our sleep cycles, routines, and relationships. It’s hard enough to navigate all the unpredictable challenges of the first few months. Where does a parent start figuring out their job description for the next eighteen years?

Parenting without a clear job description means the ups and downs of each child shape the parent, as well as each parent’s sensitivity to past relationship experiences and their parenting partner. Parenting led by emotional responses to each child can leave a parent floundering. Without a clear direction, parents risk leaving children without mature leadership. To begin clarifying our job description, a good place to start is with the goals that guide us.

Clarifying the Goal of Parenting—Restoring Character Over Happiness

In this era of intensive parenting, with an anxious focus on children, many parents are left with the unrealistic goal of raising happy and successful children. I wonder what first comes to mind for you as you reflect on your purpose as a parent and your goal for your children? Are they realistic goals? Do they factor in life realities, and how do we prepare our children to manage them? Do our goals include children’s development of good character?

I have followed the work of family therapist and researcher Phillip Klever[i] for many years. He’s conducted fascinating research examining what helps families function well over time. He followed 50 couples over 20 years and has teased out the impact of parents' goal-setting. The parents who did best had clear, balanced goals—not just for their children, but for themselves as well. These weren’t parents chasing perfection or control. Instead, they were guiding their families with intention. And the effect? Their families showed fewer signs of stress and emotional struggle. Drawing from this work, we can contrast different levels of parenting goals.

Higher-order goals stem from clear values and a focus on long-term growth. Such parents prioritize responsibility, self-regulation, and problem-solving, aiming to build character and internal resources over external success. They practice accepting short-term discomfort (like letting a child struggle) for longer-term outcomes.

In contrast, many modern parenting goals are reactive and image-driven, shaped by stress and fear. These focus on external validation—grades, trophies, good behavior—rather than character. They seek short-term ease and control, not long-term resilience. When these goals fail, parents may become emotionally over-involved or withdraw, unsure how to respond to setbacks. Parents shouldn’t feel blamed if they recognize that their goals have centered on success and happiness. These goals have become deeply embedded in the social comparison culture that surrounds us. It is, however, worth pausing to reconsider what we are aiming for.

The essence of higher-order parenting goals is fostering character and maturity. There is an emphasis on helping children manage anxiety rather than removing stress, promoting independence and critical thinking over obedience or image. Crucially, these parents understand that their own emotional functioning shapes the family, so they work on themselves to support their children’s growth. They take their parenting leadership seriously. So what does this shift in parenting goals look like in practice?

A Parent Job Description—Two Ways of Leading

Source: Photo by Markus Winkler on Unsplash

We see a growing pattern in both families and schools: when a child begins to struggle, the instinct is to respond with more involvement—more oversight, more organizing, and more attempts to motivate. This stems from a good-hearted desire to help, but on its own, the goal of helping a struggling child is not a helpful job description. Our higher-order goal is to relate to children supportively and give them space to grow inner character. The challenge is not to do nothing, but to step back just enough to allow the child to engage with the natural consequences of their actions—and begin developing the internal resources they’ll need for adulthood.

Consider the contrast between an anxiously child-focused job description and a parent self-development job description:

To resolve my child’s distress
OR tolerate enough upset for them to learn to manage emotions

To solve my child’s problems
OR invite their problem-solving

To pull my child away from risk
OR set boundaries while allowing mistakes and learning

To make my child happy/successful/popular
OR be a consistent, caring, principled presence

To make my child my project
OR live a principled life that serves as a steady example.

Meeting Our Children’s Needs, Not Their Wants—Finding the Right Level of Support

Parents want to support their child’s development of resourcefulness and responsible independence, and to support their child being comfortable in their own skin rather than being a people pleaser or a rebel.

Reactive parenting constantly responds to a child’s wants, whereas more mature parenting responds to their needs. I acknowledge that one of the most challenging aspects for parents to determine is their child’s specific needs at each stage of their development.

Research psychiatrist Murray Bowen acknowledged this challenge for every parent whose “overprotective energy is directed more by their anxiety than the reality needs of the child.”[ii]

How do I choose the right amount of support each child needs from me, and when it is too much or too little? Some clarity about our job description can help us to answer this question.

A Job Description for a Parent Who’s Working on Their Own Maturity

Source: Photo by Ana Curcan on Unsplash

How would you write your “parent job description” in light of what you’ve been reading?

By cultivating our own steadiness (differentiation of self), we better support each child’s growth into a resilient, values-driven young person—equipped to navigate life’s challenges and contribute positively to their relationships.

In my previous writing[iii], I said, “Grown-up parents help grow-up children.” Children benefit enormously from our efforts to steady ourselves, to hold our value-based boundaries, and to stay connected in supportive, not stifling, ways.

Our job description is essentially to be mature leaders who prepare children for adulthood. Whatever our children's age, we aim to cultivate their progress to increase their capacity for their next stage of life.

This is summarized well in this reminder from family systems scholar, Dr. Michael Kerr[iv], emphasizing that the “appropriate structure of families is that parents are in charge. This involves reality-driven functioning for the child until the child matures sufficiently not to require it.”

Put simply, we parents lead by supporting our children to the point where they no longer need our assistance. Yes, they need our love and interest throughout life, but our role is to let them go gradually. I acknowledge that this is no small task. None of us will get it right all the time. What matters is the ongoing effort to lead with goals and principles, and to love in a way that helps our children gradually learn to stand on their own.

item.title: What if Your Adult Child Needs You to Be the Villain?
item.description:
Parenting

What if Your Adult Child Needs You to Be the Villain?

When acknowledging the past doesn’t let a parent leave the defendant’s chair.

Posted August 17, 2026

Key points
  • Some parents apologize and change, yet still remain permanently cast as the offender.
  • Keeping a parent in a villain role can protect an adult child from more complicated truths about the present.
  • Healing requires accountability for the past without making one person responsible for the future.

If you have read any of my past posts, you may have heard me say that the only perfect people are in the cemetery. What I mean is that, as human beings, for as long as we are alive, we are prone to making mistakes because life is all about trial-and-error learning.

During a recent parent coaching session, a mother I’ll call Sarah said something that stopped me cold: “How many years am I supposed to remain on trial?” Her 36-year-old son Daryl had legitimate grievances. Sarah had been highly critical when he was a teenager. She pushed too hard academically, which she regrets, and she sometimes dismissed his feelings instead of listening. Sarah has done a lot of self-recrimination about her struggles and mistakes when raising Daryl.

When Apologies Are Not Enough, But Then What?

Sarah worked with her therapist for years to gain insight, communicate more effectively with Daryl, and learn how to apologize—not the defensive "I’m sorry you feel that way" kind of apology, but the real thing. She had listened to Daryl's pain and hurt feelings, and she had changed how she spoke to him.

Yet, years later, the trial still continued for Daryl. A relationship failed with a significant other, and guess what? Sarah's parenting missteps explained it. Daryl hated his job? His mother’s criticism had destroyed his confidence. He hesitated to pursue something new? Once again, Sarah shared with me how she was summoned to the defendant’s chair. That raises an uncomfortable question: What if an adult child sometimes needs a parent to remain the villain?

Every Story Is Easier With a Villain

Human beings naturally construct stories to make sense of pain. Sometimes those stories are accurate. Parents can cause real wounds. Acknowledging that is not “parent blaming”; it is accountability. But a story that once helps explain pain can eventually begin organizing a person’s life. This sentence: "I’m struggling because of what you did to me" is a huge deal in the lives of struggling adult children and their guilt-ridden parents. What many adult children and their parents struggle to see is that this sentence can contain truth while also becoming a trap. That's right, the more flexible the thinking, the more possibilities open up for calm, constructive conversation.

Otherwise, if one person remains the fixed central explanation for what is wrong, another frightening question can be postponed: What am I going to do with my life now? If you think for a moment, the villain serves a psychological purpose. As long as Mom or Dad remains responsible for today’s unhappiness, the adult child doesn’t have to fully confront uncertainty, disappointing choices, missed opportunities, relationship patterns, or the terrifying freedom of deciding what comes next. By the way, many adult children have opened up to me about the slippery slope of getting sucked into this "My parents are the villains" mentality. It has been heartwarming to work with their parents and adult children to overcome this mutually self-limiting narrative.

The Apology That Never Quite Pays the Debt

The idea that a parent's apology "just won't cut it" is one of the dynamics behind my book, You Ruined My Life—Now You Owe Me!: How to Stop Rescuing, Reduce Conflict, and Help Your Adult Child Move Forward. I have seen many cases where the “debt” isn’t always financial. Sometimes what is owed is perpetual remorse, but often when a parent apologizes, the adult child wants another conversation. And that door opening to more conversation is a great thing unless it leads to endless litigation of blame where the parent listens, and old grievances repeatedly surface.

Many parents come to me sharing stories of change, yet the original indictment remains. Respecting the adult children's perspective, what parents perceive as change often doesn't come across to their adult children the way they hoped. Eventually, the relationship can become strangely frozen: one person is always the injured party, and the other is always the defendant. The most heartbreaking part of this story is when neither the adult child nor the parent gets to become anyone new.

You Can Own the Past Without Owning the Future

A father I’ll call Ben finally told his adult daughter, Samantha, the following: “I believe you when you tell me I hurt you. I wish I had handled many things differently. I will listen when you need to talk about that. But I can’t be responsible for what you choose to do with your life from here.” Samantha, to her credit, entered the family coaching process with Ben, and they both realized Ben's boundaries weren't meant to escape accountability. Instead, they broke new ground by recognizing the difference between responsibility and permanent sentencing.

Final Thoughts

There is nothing to sugarcoat when it comes to parents owning what is theirs to own. Adult children deserve to have genuine pain acknowledged. But adulthood eventually presents all of us with a difficult proposition: Someone else may have contributed to the wounds we carry, but they cannot heal us.

So, perhaps the goal isn’t deciding who was the hero and who was the villain. I have seen both adult children and their parents make huge leaps forward in repairing their relationships when they realize that heroes and villains can be removed from the family narrative when it comes to meaningful healing.

item.title: What Is This 'Kinda Chic' Social Media Trend?
item.description:
Social Media

What Is This 'Kinda Chic' Social Media Trend?

There are kinda good and not so good things about the "kinda chic" trend.

Posted August 17, 2026

Key points
  • People have been using "kinda chic to" describe things not traditionally considered fashionable or stylish.
  • "Kinda chic" is used to embrace mundane habits, messy things, establishing boundaries, and self-care.
  • People have also used "kinda chic" to push back against different stereotypes, norms, and expectations.
People have been using "kinda chic" to refer to things that may not traditionally be considered stylish or elegant like mundane and messy habits.
Source: New Africa / Shutterstock

Well, this is kinda interesting. More and more people have been using the phrase "kinda chic to" on TikTok, Instagram, and other social media platforms to the point that it's become kinda chic to do so. So it does make sense to see what this is kinda all about.

What Does 'Kinda Chic' Mean?

"Kinda" is a quick way of saying "kind of," because who has the time to say the word "of" these days. Meanwhile, Dictionary.com defines "chic" as "stylish or elegant." So taken together, "kinda chic to" means that something you are about to mention is sort of stylish or elegant.

Therefore, people have been finishing this phrase with something that may not be traditionally considered very fashionable or stylish. After all, you wouldn't use the phrase to describe something that's widely considered chic, such as "kinda chic to wear a $37,000 silk dress or trench coat." You'd simply say it's chic to do it, unless you want to humblebrag in any way—meaning pretend to be humble while bragging. But more on that later.

People Have Been Using 'Kinda Chic to' Do Mundane Habits

One use of the phrase has been for everyday, mundane habits. For example, it may be kinda chic to do your laundry, take out the trash, floss your teeth, or go to bed at an earlier hour. The thought here is that most people's lives—including rich and famous people's lives—are actually filled with such things. It's too much to expect anyone to always be going to elegant dinners and parties. So you might as well embrace what you are doing each day.

People Have Been Using 'Kinda Chic to' Do Messy Stuff

Another use has been for very messy things, which in theory is the opposite of chic. So, you might say that it's kinda chic to spill drinks or food on yourself, have your teeth turn blue after eating frozen blueberries or drinking a smoothie, or have a hairstyle where you looked like you inserted your finger into an electric socket. This can poke fun at your own messiness, but also accept the fact that most of us do not always look put together. And when you see, for example, celebrities close up, you realize that they can be just as frazzled and messy, if not more so.

People Have Been Using 'Kinda Chic' to Establish Boundaries and Other Self-Care

Then there's the use of "kinda chic" for well-being purposes. You may say that it's kinda chic to not drink alcohol at a party even though everyone else is doing so, or ask for less salt in your food even if it takes some extra steps. Or you may say that it is kinda chic to stay away from a particular toxic person, even if that person seems popular. The phrase is a recognition that protecting your mental, emotional, and physical health is always the cool thing to do, even when it seems to go against the grain.

People Have Been Using 'Kinda Chic' to Push Back Against Stereotypes and Societal Norms

A fourth usage has been pushing forth past different stereotypes and societal norms. These include saying that it is kinda chic to eat alone at a restaurant, remain single, have a job that's not widely considered cool, not buy things that everyone else is seemingly buying, or date someone who may make others say, "Huh?"

It's become kinda chic to defy outdated and potentially nonsensical age expectations, too. For example, Drew Barrymore posted that it's “kinda chic to be in your 50s,” even though Hollywood is notorious for favoring younger actresses. I've also heard numerous venture capitalists claim that entrepreneurs should be no older than their 20s, when there are examples like Harland Sanders starting Kentucky Fried Chicken in his 60s. So you could say that it is kinda chic to start a company at any age.

And everyone knows that there are societal expectations to do certain things by certain ages. So you may feel left behind if you haven't reached a certain status, gotten married, had kids, bought a house, or whatever by a particular age. But you could say that it is kinda chic to have your own timeline because everyone's path is kinda unique with its accompanying benefits.

People Have Been Using 'Kinda Chic' About Different Appearances

And of course you can't have a social media trend without physical appearance factoring in somehow, right? People have been using kinda chic for looks that go against the so-called norms. For example, model Ashley Graham described a photo of her doing the Victoria’s Secret catwalk as “kinda chic to know cellulite never held you back." The fashion, entertainment, and other industries can also portray people of certain demographics like age, race, and ethnicity as more or less attractive. So, if you're not one of the favored demographics, you can say it's kinda chic to be who you are and cherish your uniqueness.

Some Are Kinda Fed Up With the 'Kinda Chic' Trend

Of course, not everyone is on board with this trend. In fact, on social media, you will find those kinda annoyed by it—describing it as overused and disingenuous, with so many people just kinda getting on the bandwagon. It also can be kinda over the top when people use it to humblebrag about themselves, like saying that it is “Kinda chic to call the Upper East Side home,” when most people kinda don't have the money to do so.

As with many social media trends, there are kinda good and kinda bad sides here. It's kinda great to give people more agency to embrace their uniqueness, be themselves, shed harmful and restrictive societal stereotypes and expectations, and make for a kinda, gentler, and more accepting society. At the same time, it's kinda not so great if this is a fad that just trivializes such things and simply gives self-promoters more opportunities. So, we kinda have to see how long this lasts and what happens.

item.title: Why the Lindsay Clancy Trial Is Triggering for Many Women
item.description:
Gender

Why the Lindsay Clancy Trial Is Triggering for Many Women

What can happen when women’s concerns are dismissed.

Posted August 17, 2026

Key points
  • The details of the Lindsay Clancy case are triggering for many women.
  • Women have a long history of having their health and mental health concerns dismissed or misinterpreted.
  • Good healthcare requires curiosity when symptoms do not fit an obvious explanation.
Source: image created by chatgpt

Like many mental health clinicians, I have many clients and colleagues who are following the Lindsay Clancy case closely. But I have also found that many of us are reacting to the case in a more personal way.

Like many women, I recognize the painful experience of feeling dismissed when you know something isn't right, and the fear that comes with wondering whether anyone is truly listening. I understand the experience of telling a healthcare professional that something is wrong, not feeling heard, and wondering whether anyone will take you seriously.

The case is horrifying. It is heartbreaking. And it has understandably generated intense debate about postpartum mental illness, maternal mental healthcare, responsibility, and the criminal justice system. But there is another reason I think this case is particularly triggering for many of us. It touches something many women already know intimately: the feeling of asking for help and being unable to find it.

Women have a long history of having concerns dismissed

Many of us have sat in a doctor's office describing pain that doesn't make sense, describing exhaustion that doesn't feel like "just being tired," and thinking something isn't right. Many of us have reported changes in our bodies, frightening thoughts, neurological symptoms, severe pain, hormonal changes, or symptoms that seem impossible to explain. And many of us have been dismissed.

Research has documented gender disparities in medical care, including differences in how women's symptoms are interpreted, investigated, and treated1-4. Women (especially women of color) have historically been underrepresented in medical research, as medical knowledge has often been developed around white male bodies and then generalized to all races and genders1-2.

Women also report having symptoms dismissed or attributed to emotional causes more frequently than men2. Research examining diagnostic bias has found that women can be more likely to have unexplained physical symptoms interpreted through a psychological lens3-4. For BIPOC women, research finds even greater disparities in care5.

Pain is one particularly well-documented example. Women are more likely to experience a number of chronic pain conditions, yet research indicates that their pain is not always taken as seriously as it should be3-4. Symptoms may be attributed to stress, emotions, hormones, or other psychological explanations rather than prompting investigation by providers to figure out what could be going on.

This history matters because it shapes how women experience healthcare today.

If you've spent your entire life being told that your symptoms are exaggerated, hormonal, anxiety-related, or simply part of being a woman, you may eventually begin to question yourself. Many of my female clients will come to session after another disappointing attempt at getting medical support. They start to dismiss their own concerns: Maybe I'm overreacting. Maybe I'm being dramatic. Maybe this really is just anxiety.

Current reporting surrounding the Clancy trial has highlighted the difficulty of recognizing symptoms and the importance of coordinated maternal mental healthcare. Many of my clients are watching the Clancy trail, and seeing themselves in her experience. "That happened to me too after my first baby," one client told me last week, "I kept asking for a higher level of care and being told I didn't meet criteria. What other criteria is needed when I'm asking for help?!"

"I feel for her so much," another client said, "the feeling of being so desperate for help, feeling so alone, and having nowhere to turn."

As a therapist, I have heard versions of this story repeatedly: A woman seeks help. She knows something is wrong, and she tries to explain it. Someone minimizes it. She tries again. Eventually, she begins minimizing it herself and begins to lose trust in her own perceptions and experiences.

Women deserve healthcare that takes them seriously, even when the answer isn't immediately obvious.

Sometimes the most important thing a healthcare provider can say is “I believe you.”

We don't have to decide what happened in Lindsay Clancy's case to understand why the story is triggering for so many women. Many women recognize the frightening experience of telling a healthcare provider that something is wrong and wondering whether anyone is actually listening.

The lesson I hope we take from this case is that good healthcare requires clinical judgment. But good clinical judgment also requires curiosity. It requires asking another question when something doesn't fit. And it requires being willing to say: I don't know yet. Let's keep looking. I have said those very words to my own clients when the answer wasn't immediately obvious. And, with great humility, I sometimes find myself wondering about all the symptoms and stories I may have missed along the way: the things a client tried to tell me that I didn't fully understand at the time, and the questions I wish I had asked them in hindsight.

This trial should help us ask the right questions

The details of Clancy's case remain contested, and are not the scope of this post. A court is still considering the evidence. But we can use the conversation about the trial to ask some larger questions:

Are women being adequately screened for mental health conditions?

Are changes in symptoms being taken seriously?

What happens when a woman says, “I don't feel like myself,” and nobody knows what to do with that information?

We need to do better.

If you are experiencing a mental health crisis, call 988 OR Text HOME to 741741 to reach a trained Crisis Counselor through Crisis Text Line. Check the Psychology Today directory to find a therapist who understands postpartum depression and anxiety.
